title: Environmental Insights and Articles
subtitle: A collection of scientific and analytical articles on land restoration, desertification control, dust management, soil stability, and environmental innovation.

article1.title: Oil Mulching in Iran: A National Geographic Report on Stabilizing Shifting Sands
article1.excerpt: This article revisits National Geographic’s November 1979 report on the use of oil mulch to stabilize sand dunes near Ahvaz, Iran. The method aimed to reduce sand movement, preserve soil moisture, and create initial conditions for vegetation establishment.

article2.title: Short-Term Effects of Oil Mulch on Vegetation Dynamics in Southwest Iran
article2.excerpt: This study examines the short-term effects of oil mulch on vegetation in arid areas of southwest Iran. The findings suggest that mulching may help increase vegetation cover and reduce bare soil, while its effects on species diversity require careful monitoring.

article3.title: Modified Bentonite Mulch for Stabilizing Wind-Erodible Sands
article3.excerpt: This study explores the use of modified bentonite impregnated with petroleum-based materials as an approach to stabilizing sands vulnerable to wind erosion. The findings suggest potential applications in erosion control and reducing soil particle movement.

article4.title: Sand Dune Stabilization in the Baiji Region of Iraq
article4.excerpt: This article reviews different approaches to stabilizing sand dunes, including oil and biological mulches, native vegetation planting, and windbreaks. It emphasizes the importance of combining mechanical, biological, and management-based methods according to local climate conditions.

article5.title: Investigation of the Effect of Mulching with Petroleum Products on Water Quality
article5.excerpt: This article investigates the effects of petroleum mulch on water quality, with particular attention to heavy elements and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Short-, medium-, and long-term petroleum mulch samples from the Hamidiyeh sand dunes in Khuzestan Province, together with a sample from the Abadan Refinery, were examined under laboratory conditions. The results indicated that petroleum mulch did not significantly increase heavy-element contamination in water, while the concentrations of all investigated hydrocarbons remained below the permitted limits.
